This document describes th e functions of the Envir onmental Monitoring System in the Mark Cuban Cost 
Plus Drug Company, PBC SCADA-PCS Misc. PLC proj ect.  This document de scribes the necessary 
control logic blocks for the project and is supplemented by the Functional Specification.   
2. TERMINOLOGY 
Configuration – Setting the control software to match the hard ware modules and communication 
methods 
DCS - Distributed Control System  
EMS – Environmental Monitoring System  
HMI - Human Machine Interface 
I/O - Input / Output 
P&ID - Piping and Inst rumentation Diagram  
PID - Proportional, Integral, Deri vative (control methodology) 
PAC - Programmable Automation Controller (used for higher-level, process-type  control functionality 
compared to PLCs, approaching or equal to DCS functionality.  Sometimes the PAC and PLC 
terminology is used interchangeably.) 
PCS – Process Control System (T his project’s panel is named PC S-CP01, Process Control System 
Control Panel 01) 
PLC - Programmable Logic Controller  (used for lower-level logicc ontrol; sometimes the PAC and PLC 
terminology is used interchangeably.) 
Programming - Developing softwa re logic or source code  
SCADA – Supervisory Contro l and Data Acquisition  
VHP – Vaporized Hydrogen Peroxide  
WFI – Water for Injection

Prior to generating this Control Block Narrative cust omer documentation and pr oject deliverables were

4. EMS CONTROL DESCRIPTION 
The Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) consists  of many sensors and indicators, some of which 
are connected to the PCS PLC.  Th e PCS PLC portion of th e system includes temperature, pressure, 
humidity, hydrocarbon measurements, and VHP con centration alarm information.  Additionally, 
feedback mechanisms consisting of visual indicator lights, strobe lig hts, and audible horns are also 
included.      Since an Administrator or Mainte nance person may put any input poi nt in SIMULATE and change its 
value, it is the responsibility of this person to supervise and adjust the manually inserted value for any 
points placed in SIMULATE.  Failure to properlys upervise and adjust manually  inserted values may 
cause incorrect control functions an d may lead to e quipment damage.  
 The PCS EMS sub-system operates in only one mode: Monitoring. 
 The scaling of analog values shall follow the ranges listed in the Al arms, Hard, and Soft IO Listing 
document (MCCPDC PCS-CP01 Alarms  Hard Soft IO Listing.xlsx) 
4.1 Process Description and Strategy Design 
4.1.1 Differential Pressure Measurements 
For differential pressure, a space static pressu re sensor (PE) and a pressure differential 
indicating transmitter (PDIT) m ounted in the room, shall mon itor the space pressure.  The 
PDIT reference is measured against the Refe rence Air header to ne ar zero conditions (0 
inches of water column). 
4.1.2 Temperature Measurements 
For temperature, temperature se nsor/transmitters (TE/TIT) mount ed in the process critical 
rooms shall monitor the space temperature condition.   
4.1.3 Humidity Measurements 
For humidity, humidity sensor/t ransmitters (HE/HIT), mounted  in the process critical 
rooms shall monitor the space humidity condition.

4.3 Tasks/Routines/Functions 
The analog inputs and outputs will be scaled wi th MapIn and MapOut routines as described 
according to the MCCPDC Controller Guidelin es document and using the values in the 
MCCPDC Alarms Hard Soft IO Listing.xlsx.  For this work the following sp ecific routines are expected: 
 R105_EMS  R110_MapInLAD  R111_MapInFBD  R120_MapOutLAD  R121_MapOutFBD 
4.4 Operator Interface 
Each of the EMS input signals is displayed in  engineering units on th e HMI.  As mentioned 
previously, with the proper credentials, the input points can be simulated for calibration or other 
maintenance activities.  Similarly, given the pr oper credentials, the alarm limits for the EMS 
signals are also available for revi ew and adjustment  via the HMI. 
The visual and audible annunciators  (light trees and audible aler ts) also provide feedback to 
personnel in the area without the need to actively view an HMI screen.   
4.5 Messages and Alarming 
The EMS messages and alarms, together with other system alarms, are de scribed in the overall 
PCS system document named MCCPDC PCS-CP01 Al arms Hard Soft IO Listing.xlsx.  That 
document provides, among other de tails, the alarm text, the input point tag identifier, the alarm 
setpoint, and any time-delay associated with the alarm.  For the alarms listed here, alarm limit 
processing, time delay, etc. is handled in the PL C and not in the FactoryTalk Alarm and Events 
Server.  The alarm setpoints are not calcu lated but are static, user-adjus table values via the HMI as 
detailed in the MCCPDC PCS-CP01 Alarms  Hard Soft IO Listing.xlsx document. 
 See Section 4.1.6.1 Alarms/Beacons to see the de scription of acknowledging and resetting of 
alarms.

The PCS shall historically record quality da ta and system alarms.  All data shall be 
available to user via displays.  The logging of data points is not set in the PLC but rather 
in the FactoryTalk Historian Site Edition (SE) software product.  See MCCPDC PCS-
CP01 Alarms Hard Soft IO Listing.xlsx to determine which input, output, and internal 
points shall be configured to be logged in the FactoryTalk Historian software product.   
4.1.5 Hardwired Signals to/from Building Management System (BMS) 
4.1.5.1  BMS Common Trouble Signal (Input) 
The PCS system has an input signal from the BMS system which indicates the status of 
the BMS.  The signal is named: “BMS Common Trouble Signal” (XS-00001-03).  When 
this signal goes into the alarm state (OFF, logic 0, no voltage at the PCS-CP01 PLC input 
pin), the PCS Light Tree Amber light shall be  illuminated and an alarm banner shall be 
displayed on the PCS HMI screens.  This is  a fail-safe design which also detects a 
broken/disconnected wire or other interrupti on in the wiring connection between the PCS 
and the BMS.  4.1.5.2  PCS Common Trouble Signal to BMS (Output) 
The PCS system has a dry contact output conne ction to the BMS which alerts the BMS of 
a PCS ‘trouble’ condition.  Th e signal is named: “PCS Common Trouble Signal to BMS” 
(XI-00001-01) and will be energized in the normal condition and de-energized in the 
alarm/trouble condition.  This is a fail -safe design which also detects a 
broken/disconnected wire or other interrupti on in the wiring connection between the PCS 
and the BMS.    The PCS Common Trouble Signal to BMS w ill change from “OK” (energized) to 
“Trouble” (de-energized) when any issues arise with the PCS system itself.  This includes 
the following events: 
PCS I/O module fault PCS Analog I/O open wi re fault detected 
FactoryTalk Historian server unreachable 
 (Which would be an indicator that da ta is not being logged as expected.) 
 4.1.5.3  EMS Common Trouble Sign al to BMS (Output) 
The PCS system has a second dr y contact output connection to  the BMS which alerts the 
BMS of an EMS ‘trouble’ condition.  Th e signal named: “EMS Common Trouble Signal 
to BMS” (XI-00001-02) will be energized in the normal condition and de-energized in 
the alarm/trouble condition.  This is a fail-safe design which also detects a 
broken/disconnected wire or other interrupti on in the wiring connection between the PCS 
and BMS.  If any EMS alarm condition is present this output will de-energize.  In this 
way, the output will mimic the re d alarm beacons indicating that one or more of the EMS 
parameters have deviated from their normal operating range.  This signal does not 
include the status of the Vapo rized Hydrogen Peroxide alarms.

4.1.6.1  Alarms/Beacons 
When an alarm condition occurs, the PCS system will sense it based on its hardware inputs or it shall be notified based on softwa re inputs.  Alarms w ill trigger visual and 
audible alarm outcomes as de scribed next.  The operator  can acknowledge an alarm 
condition at any time regardless of the curr ent process value, however the point will 
remain in alarm.  Points in alarm will return to the normal state only once the alarm 
condition is no longer present (i.e., analog value has returned to within  normal limits) and 
the operator has acknowledged the alarm.  Thes e alarms are configur ed in the PCS PLC. 
 
4.1.6.2  Stack Lights 
In addition to the on-screen alarming, the PCS will illuminate the three system stack 
lights to indicate status. 
 NORMAL – GREEN light 
When all monitored room parameters (i .e., room temperature, room humidity, 
and/or differential pressure) are within the adjustable normal range, the green visual beacon shall illuminate.  
 QUALITY (alarm) – RED light 
When, after a configurablet ime delay, a room parameter (i.e., room temperature, 
room humidity, and/or differe ntial pressure) deviate fr om the normal range by the 
alarm setpoints (thresholds), the red beacon shall illuminate.  
 PCS (and BMS) SYSTEM - AMBER light  
This lamp will illuminate when  any issues arise with the PCS system itself.  This 
includes the following events: 
PCS I/O module fault PCS Analog I/O open wi re fault detected 
A stuck open/closed fault is detect ed with any of the four valves 
FactoryTalk Historian server unreachable  (Which would indicate data loggi ng is has likely been interrupted.) 
 
Additionally, the lamp will illuminate based on the description found in Section 
4.1.5.1 BMS Common Trouble Si gnal (Input).   
  
 PCS (and BMS) SYSTEM Alarm Horn  
The Alarm Status Light Horn will sound when the PCS SYSTEM is encountering 
a fault condition.  These are the samer easons the Amber light illuminates (see 
Amber light above).
